By Evan Woodbery, mlive.com
DETROIT — Scott Harris didn’t have to spend much time searching for the stretch that doomed the Detroit Tigers’ season.
That miserable May is right there for everyone to see.
The Tigers went 6-22, tumbled into last place in the American League Central and spent the rest of the summer trying to recover. They never really did, finishing 76-86 and missing the postseason for the first time in three years.
Less than 24 hours after the season ended, Harris offered his explanation for how a team that entered the year with championship aspirations wound up 10 games under .500.
“This season, and the fact that we’re sitting here right now, is a missed opportunity for this organization, plain and simple,” the Tigers’ president of baseball operations said Monday at Comerica Park. “We’ve got to get better.”
Some of those explanations are easier to quantify than others. Here’s Harris’ assessment of what went wrong.
The May meltdown
There are a lot of ways to dissect a 162-game season, but the brutal 28-game stretch early in the season was a gut punch to the Tigers’ plans to contend in 2026.
“There are a lot of reasons why we’re sitting here and not in the playoffs right now,” Harris said. “One of them really sticks out above the rest for me. You can’t go 6-22 in a month and expect to punch your ticket to the postseason at this level.”
“I think one of the things that I’m really struggling to process about this year is, in many ways, this roster performed quite well for five months, excluding May.”
Before and after May, the Tigers went 70-64. Even more notably, Harris said, they ranked second in baseball in team ERA, second in wRC+ (weighted runs created plus) and posted a plus-119 run differential.
“That’s playoff-worthy. If anything, our record probably should have been even better than 70-64, given the underlying run production and run prevention.”
Why did May happen?
Harris’ answer began with injuries.
Injuries, and a roster that couldn’t absorb them
The Tigers were hit unusually hard by injuries.
Second baseman Gleyber Torres, outfielder Kerry Carpenter, reliever Will Vest and, of course, ace starter Tarik Skubal missed most or all of the month.
Even without Skubal and Vest, run prevention generally wasn’t the biggest problem. The lineup cratered, with significant at-bats going to fill-ins like Gage Workman and Zack Short. Role players like Jahmai Jones, Zach McKinstry and Matt Vierling were pressed into larger roles while mired in prolonged slumps.
“Our roster never really saw the light of day,” Harris said. “We built a roster that we thought was talented, that many people in this room thought was really talented, and they never all actually got on the field at the same time.”
“It’s really hard to have an honest conversation about this organization in the 2026 season without noting that we put 41 players on the injured list on our 40-man roster this year,” Harris said.
“It’s not an excuse. But at some point, you get to a volume of injuries that becomes destabilizing to your ability to manage a roster. I think it did. It really hurt us in certain sections of this year.”
But Harris also said he didn’t build enough depth beyond the active roster to handle what happened.
“Upon reflection, our inability to overcome adversity in real time starts with me,” Harris said. “I didn’t build enough depth into this roster this year. The vulnerabilities in this roster got exposed in May, and it cost us.”
Harris said Detroit entered the season knowing it would become deeper as the summer progressed, with prospects like center fielder Max Clark slated to arrive later.
“I think the main mistake that I made was our depth was coming a little bit too late, basically in all facets of our roster,” Harris said.
The Tigers were also reluctant to add players who might eventually block those prospects. That left them trying short-term fixes like Short and, later, outfielder James Outman.
“We didn’t want to block young players,” Harris said. “We didn’t want to trade for depth players that were ultimately going to box Max out of the big leagues. So we were trying to thread that needle, and I think it probably was a mistake in the end.
“We probably should have just strengthened our depth and made sure that we could get through April and May intact.”
Harris said Detroit was particularly thin with up-the-middle defenders, back-end relievers and starting-pitching depth.
“We couldn’t really afford to lose back-end relievers,” he said. “We couldn’t really afford to lose starting depth. And we couldn’t really afford to have our pinch hitters’ performance sag in leverage spots.”
All that happened in May.
“Could we afford to have all (of that) happen at the same time? No, clearly not,” Harris said. “We went 6-22 that month, and so I feel very responsible for that.”
Too much mixing and matching
The Tigers have built much of their identity by playing the matchups, mixing and matching and asking players to be versatile.
But Harris suggested for the first time that they may have become too reliant on it.
When role players do well, like Andy Ibáñez in 2024 and Jahmai Jones in 2025, it’s a huge boost in high-leverage moments.
But when players in those roles struggle, as they did during key points in 2026, it can be devastating.
Harris sees the arrival of more players like Kevin McGonigle and Max Clark, who the Tigers believe can contribute both offensively and defensively and play nine innings every day, as a way to reduce that dependence.
“I think we’re probably going to start playing differently a little bit,” Harris said. “We’re going to be less reliant on pinch-hit appearances. We’re going to be less reliant on the mixing and matching because we have more two-way players growing through the system that can help us both defensively and offensively.”
Lagging in leverage
Based on their run differential, the Tigers had an expected record of 89-73, not 76-86.
Of course, baseball doesn’t work that way. But the gap between what actually happened and what their run differential suggests should have happened is one of the most perplexing storylines of 2026.
“When you take a look at our season, our run differential says one thing and our record says something very different,” Harris said.
“If we had played up to our run differential, we probably would have won the division again.”
“That doesn’t matter,” he added. “I can’t stand up here and just cite different metrics and tell you this is what we should have done and act like we did it. We didn’t do it.”
“So the question that I’m going to ask myself is: How do we play in a way that either meets or exceeds our run production and run prevention performance, our underlying performance?”
It’s no secret the Tigers won a lot of blowouts and lost a ton of close games. They went an astonishing 23-52 in games decided by two runs or fewer.
That’s largely because the Tigers performed better in low- and medium-leverage situations than they did when the leverage spiked.
The numbers were particularly stark among relievers.
Tigers relievers faced 370 batters in high-leverage situations and posted a jaw-dropping 9.21 ERA (5.62 FIP). Opponents posted an .855 OPS against them and hit a league-high 19 home runs in those situations. A staggering 21.8 percent of opposing fly balls landed in the seats. No other team was even close in that category.
Maybe that’s bad luck. But it’s also bad news for any team trying to contend.
“We really struggled in high leverage,” Harris said. “We’ve got to get to the bottom of that. We’ve got to figure out why that happens.”
Harris said sometimes the problem was that the game never should have reached a high-leverage situation in the first place.
“We’ve got to do a better job of staying out of those high-leverage situations,” Harris said.
That means looking beyond the final pitch of a loss.
“There were a number of games that we saw this year where we got walked off or our bullpen blew a late lead that I don’t think you can actually put on our bullpen,” Harris said.
“Some of them you can, for sure. But some of them you can’t.
“Some of them you can actually look deeper into the game and you could find the core issue, which was we didn’t create separation before, or we made a misplay in the third inning and coughed up one or two runs, or we made a baserunning mistake in the fifth inning,” Harris said.
“We let our opponent stay in the game, create this one- and two-run game, and then we ultimately lost it.”
Harris believes the changing makeup of the roster can help with that.
The Tigers are getting younger, faster and, in Harris’ view, more athletic. He expects that to mean better defense, more aggressive baserunning and more ways to create separation without simply waiting for a home run.
“We’re going to take the extra base. We’re also going to steal bases. And we’re also going to put a lot more pressure, and that’s all going to contribute to creating separation when we’re not hitting,” Harris said.
“We’re still going to hit, but we’re also going to be able to flex different muscles at different times that can help us stay out of those high-leverage situations.”
Harris said the Tigers are already conducting what he called a “pre-mortem” on the 2027 roster, trying to anticipate next year’s vulnerabilities before they arise.
“What if this happens? What are we going to do? What if this happens? What are we going to do?” Harris said.
That includes underperformance as well as injuries.
“If a guy gets out of the gate really slow, what are we going to do?” Harris said. “Those are the questions we have to ask ourselves.
“When I talk about learning lessons from the season, that’s one of the lessons that I’ve learned.”

ATLANTA -- When Walt Weiss sends Chris Sale to the mound for Game 1 of the National League Wild Card Series on Tuesday afternoon, he’ll have the same confidence he possessed more than a quarter of a century ago, when he was playing behind John Smoltz, Tom Glavine and Greg Maddux in postseason games.
“There’s a different feeling when a guy like that is taking the mound,” Weiss said. “We felt it those years with the Big Three, and I felt it at other times in my career. I felt it in Oakland with Dave Stewart. I think it elevates the room the day that guy is pitching.”
Weiss made three straight trips to the playoffs as Atlanta’s shortstop from 1998-2000, and he’s experienced the postseason seven of the past eight years as the team’s bench coach. So, Braves playoff baseball is nothing new for him.
But, for Sale, this will be an experience he has long awaited.
The 37-year-old left-hander’s back prevented him from pitching in the postseason during his 2024 NL Cy Young Award season. But the splendid year he has produced during this third season with Atlanta will be enriched when he throws the first pitch of this Wild Card Series against the Phillies on Tuesday at 2 p.m. ET (NBC/Peacock).
“I love pitching here in Atlanta,” Sale said. “I love pitching in front of these fans, and being able to do it in the postseason makes it that much more special.”
Sale’s greatest postseason moment occurred when he concluded the 2018 World Series for the Red Sox by striking out each of the three batters he faced in the ninth inning of Game 5. His most recent playoff experience occurred in 2021, when, two months after returning from Tommy John surgery, he made three frustrating starts for Boston.
Five years later, Sale is in a far different position. After injuries limited him to a total of 151 innings from 2020-23, the Red Sox essentially gave up on him and sent him to Atlanta prior to the 2024 season. The lanky lefty flourished that year, and has continued to get better. The 2.16 ERA he produced this year ranked third in MLB, and it stands as the fifth-best mark produced by any Braves pitcher who has made at least 25 starts in any season going back to 1920.
So, there truly is reason to think this year’s postseason experience might be different. Sale has constructed a 7.24 ERA in seven previous playoff starts. His struggles weren’t restricted to the 2021 experience. He posted a 6.87 ERA in the four postseason starts he made in 2017 and ‘18. He allowed seven earned runs in one and lasted fewer than five innings in two others.
“I think you learn that it's just about harnessing the energy,” Sale said. “I learned this from David Tollett, my college coach [at Florida Gulf Coast University] -- you can't be better than you are. You can't play above what you possess, and sometimes you go out there and try to do too much, and actually do less.”
The opponents and pitching matchups Sale drew over the past two months prepared him for what he could encounter over the next few weeks. While posting a 2.36 ERA over his final seven starts, he pitched against four playoff teams (Yankees, Brewers, Dodgers and twice against the Phillies) and one (D-backs) that nearly made the postseason.
Within this same stretch, Sale matched up against top-flight starters Gerrit Cole, Jacob Misiorowski, Yoshinobu Yamamoto, Cristopher Sánchez and Aaron Nola.
“He’s been nothing short of amazing for us,” Braves first baseman Matt Olson said. “I wouldn’t want anybody else taking the mound for us tomorrow.”
Sale certainly has reason to enter this assignment with confidence. He posted a 2.08 ERA in four starts against the Phillies this season, and the Braves won each of those contests.
If he can garner similar results on Tuesday, there’s a good chance this won’t be the only postseason start he will make this year.
“He presents a whole set of problems, but we've seen him a [few times],” Phillies interim manager Don Mattingly said. “We haven't been great with him, but we'll see. Tomorrow is a new day.”

SAN DIEGO — The Chicago Cubs are again turning to left-hander Matthew Boyd to begin their postseason.
Boyd, who got the Game 1 start in last year’s wild-card series against the San Diego Padres, will again get the ball when the Cubs open their rematch Tuesday, this time at Petco Park. The Cubs also could have started right-hander Kevin Gausman but opted for the lefty. Boyd held the Padres to one run in 4 1/3 innings in Game 1 last season at Wrigley Field.
“The first two months of the season were certainly interrupted and not smooth, but since then he’s gotten into a routine and consistency, that is what I think Matthew offers,” manager Craig Counsell said Monday after their team workout. “Playoff starts are a challenge. Matthew’s experienced in that and had good experiences last year with it for us and look for him to do the same tomorrow.”
Since returning from meniscus surgery June 25, Boyd posted a 3.42 ERA in his final 17 starts, allowing three earned runs or fewer in 12 of those outings.
Counsell didn’t provide specifics on who could start Games 2 or 3, the latter if necessary Thursday. Gausman is expected to pitch at some point in the series. His left shoulder injury sustained in his final regular-season start Wednesday created some uncertainty about whether he would be available this playoff round. The Cubs feel Gausman’s shoulder is trending well but isn’t fully in the clear, making a Tuesday start not a realistic option.
The Cubs are expected to carry 12 pitchers on their wild-card roster. Left-hander Shota Imanaga is also expected to factor into the Cubs’ pitching plans this series, though Counsell cautioned he didn’t know whether that would be as a starter or a reliever. Right-hander Clay Holmes wasn’t at his best down the stretch, but the Cubs anticipate him providing bulk in some capacity this series, whether that’s in a start or multiple innings out of the bullpen.
The best-of-three series allows Counsell to fully deploy all his pitchers as needed, whether it’s using starters out of the bullpen for multiple frames or even one-inning appearances. The Cubs will seek the best matchups and pockets of hitters for their pitchers to face.
“I look at these games kind of in this context that we’re talking about the urgency is you have 27 outs, we’ve got to figure out how to get 27 outs,” Counsell said. “The order that that happens — starter, reliever, closer, setup man — those words don’t matter. We’re just trying to get 27 outs.”
The Cubs’ pitching plans beyond Game 1 will be dictated by whether they win or lose the opener. It’ll be all hands on deck Wednesday for Game 2 if they don’t pull out the win Tuesday.
“It doesn’t matter how anything happens tomorrow, like aesthetically, it just matters that we win, that’s the bottom line,” Counsell said. “Because we’ve got to win two games in the next three days and so how anybody does, how anything happens, it doesn’t matter. You’ve got to win the game. And I think you probably lean more on the process over 162 games because you have to. But when you get to a two-out-of-three series to play the next game, your thoughts have to change a little bit.”
In a rematch of last year’s wild-card matchup, a venue change presents an added challenge for the Cubs against a Padres team with one of the best home records in baseball — 51-30 at Petco Park this year compared to 40-41 on the road.
The Cubs haven’t decided yet whether Alex Bregman is feeling well enough to start at third base or if they keep using him as the designated hitter to reduce the risk as he continues to play with multiple facial fractures. He took grounders at third base during live batting practice Monday, an encouraging development.
Bregman’s quick return gives the Cubs’ lineup added juice.
“I definitely think that fires you up,” Pete Crow-Armstrong said Monday. “Knowing him and how wonderfully crazed he is just about his work and how much he loves the game, not really surprising. Not to put a damper on how cool it is that he is coming back after eight facial fractures and whatnot, like, I’m just not surprised. He lives for this kind of baseball.”

For the 14th straight year, the Dodgers are postseason-bound.
Winners of three of the past six World Series, the Dodgers are looking to continue their reign. The back-to-back defending champions are bidding for the Major Leagues' first three-peat since the Yankees won three straight titles from 1998-2000.
The Dodgers, the No. 2 seed in the National League, are just about at full strength now that the likes of Shohei Ohtani, Andy Pages and Roki Sasaki have returned from the injured list, but there are several other compelling storylines to follow before the postseason.
Here's what to watch as the NL West-champion Dodgers forge their path back to the Fall Classic:
What could the postseason roster look like?
The strength of the Dodgers' pitching staff is the rotation, so expect them to carry more starters than they need and get creative with using some of them in relief. Manager Dave Roberts indicated that the team may carry only 12 pitchers to make room for an additional position player on the bench in the NL Division Series.
It may be premature to pencil in Josue De Paula, as the organization’s top prospect has played in only 11 big league games. But the Dodgers liked what they saw, and he could be an impact lefty bat off the bench.
Catchers (2): Will Smith, Hunter Feduccia
First baseman (1): Freddie Freeman
Second baseman (1): Tommy Edman
Shortstop (1): Mookie Betts
Third baseman (1): Max Muncy
Outfielders (3): Teoscar Hernández, Andy Pages, Kyle Tucker
Utility/bench (3): Kiké Hernández, Miguel Rojas, Josue De Paula, Hyeseong Kim
Two-way player (1): Shohei Ohtani
Starters (4): Yoshinobu Yamamoto, Tarik Skubal, Blake Snell, Tyler Glasnow
Relievers (9): Edwin Díaz, Tanner Scott, Edgardo Henriquez, Alex Vesia, Evan Phillips, Roki Sasaki, Kris Bubic, Brock Stewart
When does the postseason begin?
The NL Division Series begin on Saturday.
Who could be the Dodgers' NLDS opponent? 
The Dodgers won their 13th NL West title in the past 14 seasons and secured a first-round bye, so they will play the winner of the Wild Card Series between the Braves and the Phillies.
Against which teams do the Dodgers have home-field advantage?
The Dodgers have home-field advantage over every team in the postseason field except the Brewers, who finished the regular season with the best record in the Majors.
What will the postseason rotation look like?
Yamamoto, Skubal, Snell and Glasnow make up this year's Big Four. The rotation order is yet to be determined. One consideration is that Yamamoto is accustomed to starting on at least five days' rest, whereas the other three are comfortable starting on four days' rest. That makes Yamamoto likely to start Game 1 of the NLDS because he would be available for a potential Game 5 on his normal rest. 
What's the latest on Ohtani's status?
Ohtani was activated from the 15-day IL and hit in the Dodgers' final five games, going 5-for-21 (.238) with eight strikeouts and one walk. Roberts described the performance as Ohtani showing some rust and said the team does not have any health concerns with him. 
Which injured players could return?   
The Dodgers hope that Henriquez, who has emerged as an important leverage arm, can return for the postseason after his regular season came to a premature end due to lower back discomfort. He will face hitters during the bye week, and as long as he comes away feeling good, he will be activated for the NLDS.
Which roster spots may be up for grabs?
The final spot on the bench is far from set in stone. The Dodgers could carry De Paula, but Dalton Rushing, Alex Call and Hyeseong Kim are additional options. This decision could come down to whether they want to use that bench spot on a potential impact bat or someone who brings enhanced speed and/or defense to the table. If L.A. carries fewer than 13 pitchers, that would open an additional bench spot.
The bullpen should also have some openings. If Henriquez does not recover in time for the postseason, that opens an additional spot. Justin Wrobleski, Sasaki and Emmet Sheehan were starters for most of the season, but they will be relief options in the postseason. But Wrobleski was inconsistent in the second half, and the Dodgers have other left-handers who may be more reliable in leverage, such as Bubic.
Who will close out games?
Díaz was supposed to resolve the Dodgers' ninth-inning troubles, but he has only added to them in his first year in L.A. Since returning from the IL, he has looked much better, which could have him back in the mix to close out games. The Dodgers may be more likely to play the matchups instead of going with a set closer in the postseason. Based on regular-season performance, Scott and Henriquez are two of the top options to pitch in save situations. Perhaps Sasaki could reprise his postseason closer role if needed.

The best time of the baseball year is finally here. The playoffs begin Tuesday, with a quadruple-header of wild-card games on tap. The schedule for each series' first two games is identical.
Let's break down how each team got here, how they can win, X-factors, series predictions and more before the wild-card round begins.
AL: CWS-HOU • BOS-NYY | NL: PHI-ATL • CHC-SD
No. 6 Philadelphia Phillies vs. No. 3 Atlanta Braves
Projected starters
(all times ET)
Game 1, 2 p.m. Tuesday (NBC/PCK): Jesús Luzardo (PHI) vs. Chris Sale (ATL)
Game 2, 2 p.m. Wednesday (NBC/PCK): Cristopher Sánchez (PHI) vs. Tyler Mahle (ATL)
Game 3, TBD*: Aaron Nola (or Zack Wheeler on four days' rest) (PHI) vs. Grant Holmes (ATL)
(*if necessary)
How they got here
Phillies: It was a Dr. Jekyll and Mr. Hyde type of season for the Phillies, to say the least. For the second time in five seasons, an in-season managerial firing was needed to light a fire under an underperforming veteran roster that appeared to be letting their window close. But the Phillies, like they've done before, found a way to get themselves going on the back of their starting rotation. The Phillies didn't make it easy on themselves in September, going 10-14 down the stretch and needing to win their regular-season finale against the Rays to punch their ticket to the postseason. But now that they're in, this veteran group will look to show that they're better than the past month suggests.
Braves: It was a reassuring year in Atlanta, a much-needed reminder that no, this era of Braves baseball was not over after their disastrous, postseason-less 2025. A change in manager, from the now-retired Brian Snitker to the endearingly pugnacious Walt Weiss, set the tone. As did a major refresh of Atlanta's coaching staff. That turnover, in contrast with the continuity on the roster, proved crucial as Atlanta waltzed to its first division title since 2023.
Big campaigns from metronomic first baseman Matt Olson and 2025 NL Rookie of the Year Drake Baldwin shocked nobody. The same was true for ace Chris Sale, certain to be voted an NL Cy Young finalist. But few would've predicted Michael Harris II leading the team in bWAR with a dynamic, consistent offensive season. Role players such as Mauricio Dubón, Mike Yastrzemski and Dominic Smith all delivered critical production to help offset underwhelming seasons from the likes of Ozzie Albies and Austin Riley.
Ronald Acuña Jr., that wonderfully mercurial burst of baseballing light, might've fit into that last group if not for an otherworldly September in which he clocked seven homers with a .950 OPS. That renaissance continuing into October would be a game-changer for the Braves, whose 2021 title came with Acuña sidelined.
X-factors
Phillies: Trea Turner
The regular season wasn't kind to shortstop Trea Turner, who recorded the worst season of his career. But the thing about the postseason is that it allows players who have not yet written the final story on their season to become heroes. And if the Phillies want to move past Atlanta and reach the NLDS for the fifth straight year, Turner finding his rhythm would be a welcomed sight for the team's offense. Turner has a .733 OPS off Sale in 25 career at-bats and a very respectable .863 OPS off Mahle in 25 career at-bats.
Braves: Tyler Mahle
Chris Sale is going to start Game 1 for Atlanta, and he's probably going to be pretty good. That feels as bankable as anything in our topsy-turvy world. But Mahle, set to throw Game 2, has been one of the game's most reliable starters since he joined the Braves from a zip-less San Francisco team at the deadline. The veteran righty posted a 1.99 ERA with Atlanta, allowing one earned or fewer in seven of his nine starts.
Mahle's most recent start, however, was a relative stinker. He surrendered five runs and struck out just four at home against an undermanned Reds lineup. And the underlying metrics, it should be said, are a bit more skeptical about Mahle's prospects. That's understandable. He doesn't throw that hard or strike out oodles of hitters. He hasn't conjured more swing-and-miss or meaningfully lowered opponents' hard-hit rate as a Brave. And yet, Mahle has found a way to find outs. Whether he can do so against Philly's bats will be huge.
How they win
Phillies: Can any team in baseball go toe-to-toe with Philly's starting rotation? With the quartet of Wheeler, Sánchez, Luzardo and Nola, the Phillies should have the advantage in a three-, five- or seven-game series. So while their offense is more of a wild card (pun intended), this team should be able to count on its starter giving them a chance to win every time out. And if that foursome gets hot, it's not outlandish to believe they could carry Philly on another deep postseason run.
Braves: It has been a restful week for the Braves, who were able to sit back, relax and line up their starting rotation for this wild-card series. The same cannot be said for Philly, which needed every last out to clinch on the regular season's final day. For the Phillies, the sense of exhaustion is real and gives Atlanta a legitimate advantage.
But it all starts with Sale. If he cruises like he's capable of in Game 1, that puts Atlanta in the catbird seat. Only one team in the current playoff format (the 2025 Yankees) came back to win a wild-card series after losing the first game.
Series prediction: Braves in 3
No. 6 Chicago White Sox vs. No. 3 Houston Astros
Projected starters
(all times ET)
Game 1, 5 p.m. ET Tuesday (PCK/NBCSN): David Sandlin (CWS) vs. Peter Lambert (HOU)
Game 2 5 p.m. ET Wednesday (PCK/NBCSN): Sean Burke (CWS) vs. Hunter Brown (HOU)
Game 3, TBD*: Davis Martin (CWS) vs. Hayden Wesneski (HOU)
(*if necessary)
How they got here
White Sox: The White Sox have been easily one of the best stories of the 2026 regular season, reaching the postseason for the first time since 2021. Chicago became the first team in MLB history to reach the postseason following three consecutive 100-loss seasons, capturing the third AL wild-card spot. The offense, led by first-time All-Stars Miguel Vargas and Munetaka Murakami, was the driving force behind the Sox's success. Chicago finished the season with a top-five offense in MLB.
The fact that the White Sox didn't win the AL Central might come as a disappointment, considering they were in first place for the majority of the second half. Still, it's undeniable that any result that puts them in the playoffs is a huge victory for the organization and a fan base that has been waiting for competitive baseball.
Astros: For a franchise that has accomplished so much over the past decade, there's something shameful, even humiliating about raising the 2026 AL West banner. That's because these Astros are, by record, the single worst division winner in the sport's long past. Before Sunday, no team with a .500 record or below had ever reached the postseason. But Houston rewrote history thanks to an MVP-caliber season from Yordan Alvarez and a tidal wave of mediocrity from its AL West counterparts. Their inclusion in the October jamboree is more an indictment of the Texas Rangers and the Seattle Mariners than anything else, but the Astros at least ended on a high note with their 9-0 win over the A's on Sunday.
Houston also deserves a morsel of credit for refurbishing its season after a disastrous April. Reaching .500 with the fourth-worst starting staff by ERA — only the Reds, A's and Rockies were worse — is also an accomplishment worth commending, a testament to something. Where would this club be without Peter Lambert, whose 3.87 ERA in 153 2/3 innings offered the only semblance of stability for a roster constantly in flux?
Things got sad enough, discombobulated enough, that in August owner Jim Crane relieved GM Dana Brown of his duties. There's an overwhelming expectation that skipper Joe Espada won't be back next year, either. It's difficult to be optimistic about Houston's very uncertain future. But in the random present of playoff baseball, anything is possible — especially when you employ the best hitter on the planet.
X-factors
White Sox: Munetaka Murakami
Munetaka Murakami is a game-changer, and his presence in the White Sox's lineup is a huge advantage in the postseason. The White Sox's rookie slugger burst onto the scene in 2026, hitting 35 home runs and providing instant impact in his first season after coming over from Japan. But following a midseason hamstring injury, the league seemed to adjust to him; Murakami finished with a slashline of .184/.328/.423 and 11 homers since Aug 1. Still, he has the type of power that can change a series by himself, and with three homers in the final week of the season, he appears to be coming out of his second-half slump. If Murakami has rediscovered his power stroke, it could change this series.
Astros: Isaac Paredes
Yordan Alvarez is currently the best hitter on earth. He cannot, under any circumstances, be allowed to dictate proceedings during this series. Chicago must make somebody else in Houston's mediocre lineup beat them. If there's a base open with Alvarez up, he should just stroll straight to first every time.
That puts a mountain of pressure on Paredes. The stocky third baseman has been hitting right behind Alvarez for most of the season and has, for the most part, showed well. He's a supremely weird hitter, one who rarely hits the ball hard or barrels it up. But Paredes doesn't whiff, doesn't punch out and has a preternatural knack for pulling the ball in the air. Expect him to come up multiple times in big spots with runners on.
How they win
White Sox: The White Sox's offense has carried them all season, and if they hope to advance to the ALDS against their division rival, they'll have to slug their way there. Vargas, Murakami and shortstop Colson Montgomery each finished the season with more than 30 longballs, and the Sox finished fifth in MLB in homers. For a team built to slug, Daikin Park in Houston isn't the worst environment to play in on the road. Chicago's power-packed lineup has shown that if they're hitting the ball out of the ballpark, offensively, they can play with anyone.
Astros: Houston desperately needs offensive contributions from someone besides Alvarez. Maybe it's the aforementioned Paredes or the en fuego Yainer Díaz. Perhaps Jose Altuve, 36 years old and in full decline, has one magical month left in his Hall of Fame career. But with such a tattered pitching staff, the Astros need to score to win. They also need to win the Hunter Brown start; he's far and away their best starter. They need a lot, frankly. And yet, much weirder October things have happened inside that East Texas thunderdome over the past decade.
Series prediction: Astros in 3
No. 5 Boston Red Sox vs. No. 4 New York Yankees
Projected starters
(all times ET)
Game 1, 8 p.m. Tuesday (NBC/PCK): Payton Tolle (BOS) vs. Cam Schlittler (NYY)
Game 2, 8 p.m. Wednesday (NBC/PCK): Sonny Gray (BOS) vs. Max Fried (NYY)
Game 3, TBD*: Ranger Suárez (BOS) vs. Gerrit Cole (NYY)
(*if necessary)
How they got here
Red Sox: Odysseus would be proud. What a winding, bizarre and tumultuous road it has been for the Sox. Boston began the year like a snail on Unisom, posting a lackluster 9-17 record through April 24. That precipitated a dramatic, Red Wedding-style culling, in which manager Alex Cora and several other staff members were relieved of their duties. Extended injury list stints for the team's two most important pieces, outfielder Roman Anthony and 2025 Cy Young runner-up Garrett Crochet, made a turnaround feel awfully unlikely. On July 24, the Sox lost a rubber match in Colorado and traveled home 14 games under .500. Their postseason odds wallowed around 10%.
Then, everything changed. It began with a home mop against the Yanks and fully kicked into gear when the Red Sox hit the road for a three-city swing the first week of July. They went 9-0 on that trip before winning six straight at home. That 15-game streak catapulted them back into contention and the good graces of an understandably unplugged fan base. Between July 3 and Aug. 7, the Sox went a ridiculous 32-5, trampolining from 14 games under .500 to 13 games over. Fenway was a zoo. Nothing could go wrong. Boston ballfans beamed once again.
The heater earned Cora's replacement, Chad Tracy, the full-time gig. It also afforded the Sox a relatively comfortable September. It's worth noting, though, that Boston has not played particularly crisply since cooling off from the volcanic run, with a 21-22 record since Aug. 8. Ultimately, their final numbers and standing in the American League are not shocking or unexpected, even though Boston's odyssey was wonky beyond comparison.
Yankees: For all the stress, the drama, the hand-wringing, for all the injuries and under-performance, 2026 was a relatively straightforward season in YankeeLand. A lot, it should be said, went wrong. Reigning AL MVP Aaron Judge has played just seven games since May. Giancarlo Stanton hasn't played since April. Max Fried and Carlos Rodón each missed about two months. Young players such as Anthony Volpe, Jasson Dominguez and Austin Wells regressed offensively. Gerrit Cole, coming back from Tommy John, didn't fully recapture his frontline best.
And yet, here the Yankees are, with 93 wins and in an identical place to where they finished last year. That's thanks to breakout campaigns from homegrown pieces such as Cam Schlittler (the AL Cy Young favorite) and Ben Rice (41 home runs and a .897 OPS). Closer David Bednar has been dynamite. Cody Bellinger has been a rock. Skipper Aaron Boone kept the train on the tracks. Three games at home against the Red Sox await. Beyond that looms an ALDS against a daunting division foe. We've been here before.
The largest difference, of course, is the uncertainty swirling around Judge. The Yankees' captain missed three months due to a rib problem, came back for a week, strained his calf and went back on the shelf. Boone says he's preparing for a wild-card round without Judge. Judge says he plans to play. What sort of magic this reduced version of Judge can conjure is easily the juiciest storyline ahead of this rivalry showdown. That said, this series, like this Yankees season, is probably going to be dictated by the pitchers.
X-factors
Red Sox: Roman Anthony
It has been an odd season for the 22-year-old, who missed last year's wild-card festivities due to injury. In March, Anthony was a late addition to Team USA's WBC roster. He shined on that grand stage, impressing his more established teammates and earning plaudits from a coaching staff of hardball lifers. That only ratcheted up the hype on a player expected to carry a franchise less than a year after he became legally permitted to drink a beer.
So when Anthony started slowly, disappointment bubbled. Then, on May 4, he tore a ligament in his finger; that kept him out of action until Aug. 30. A lot happened in the interim, most of which Anthony spent rehabbing at the team's complex in Florida. Since returning, he has looked promising, tantalizingly close to unleashing the full assortment of his talents upon the league. Now, with Willson Contreras banged up and either unavailable or restricted, the pressure returns to Anthony's young shoulders.
Yankees: Luis García Jr.
García was a curious character for the Yankees to shape their trade deadline around. Instead of acquiring a piece that filled an obvious void (righty stick with defensive value or versatility), GM Brian Cashman opted to add the most dynamic hitter possible. New York landed on García, who was in the midst of an offensive breakout under a new Washington Nationals regime.
For a month, that plan bore fruit, with the Dominican slugger posting an .846 OPS in August. But since then, the wheels have fallen off, with García's chase rate skyrocketing. His September OPS started with a 5. He has homered just twice since Aug. 26. He doesn't have an extra-base hit since Sept. 10. There's a chance, given Boston's bevy of southpaws and New York's DH surplus, that he doesn't start every game. But García will get his chances, and whether he comes up big might swing the series.
How they win
Red Sox: Boston's pitching staff is the only one in baseball that ranks in the top five in both home run rate and walk rate. That's a rare combo. Usually, throwing the ball in the strike zone more often leads to more hard contact. But these Red Sox hurlers, for whatever reason, have threaded that needle perfectly. No team in the league has allowed fewer homers. However, no team has hit more than the Yankees. Boston revitalized its season behind pitching and defense, keeping the scores low and the games close. Doing so here will give them the best chance of authoring an upset.
Yankees: No American League team can compete with New York's starting staff. But the Yankees need more than dominance from Schlittler, Fried and Cole. They need length. The bridge to Bednar is unsteady. So the longer the starters go, the rosier that path looks. Offensively, the Yankees need a big swing or two from their right-handed bats against Boston's left-handed arms. That could come from a banged-up Judge or Stanton. It could come from veteran southpaw-killer Paul Goldschmidt, trade-acquisition Heliot Ramos or rookie shortstop George Lombard Jr. If it comes from the beleaguered Anthony Volpe, the tri-state area will lose its collective marbles. But somebody, anybody who stands on the right side of the batter's box has to make an impact.
Series prediction: Yankees in 3
No. 5 Chicago Cubs vs. No. 4 San Diego Padres
(all times ET)
Projected starters
Game 1, 10 p.m. Tuesday (PCK/NBCSN): Shota Imanaga (CHC) vs. Michael King (SD)
Game 2, 10 p.m. Wednesday (PCK/NBCSN): Clay Holmes (CHC) vs. Nick Pivetta (SD)
Game 3, TBD*: Matthew Boyd (CHC) vs. Walker Buehler or Casey Mize or Robbie Ray (SD)
(*if necessary)
How they got here
Cubs: It was Pete Crow-Armstrong's world, and the rest of us just lived in it. Chicago's 24-year-old center fielder went fully supersonic this year, cranking 45 homers, swiping 41 bags and delivering a .945 OPS with his typically elite outfield defense. He will win the NL MVP, and it might be unanimous. That performance shaped and guided and defined this Cubs' season, electrifying an offense that led baseball in OPS, K/BB rate and runs per game.
Alex Bregman's arrival via free agency, too, cannot be understated. He struggled mightily for the first few months, with his extended schneid at one point eliciting boos from a frustrated Wrigley crowd. But since July 12, Bregman leads all qualified National League hitters in OPS. His experience, comportment and leadership, by all accounts, have also had a meaningful impact on Crow-Armstrong.
But pitching woes, in both the rotation and the bullpen, kept Chicago from ever seriously threatening the Brewers for the NL Central title. The Cubs started the year on something of a roller coaster, with two 10-game winning streaks and a 10-game losing streak before the calendar flipped to June. They'll enter October on something of an ice floe, with 15 runs scored in their final six contests.
Padres: San Diego has the best record in baseball since July 24. The day before, the Pads lost a rubber match in Atlanta to fall to three games under. 500. That pushed the club four games adrift of a wild-card spot, with the Cardinals, Pirates, Marlins, Nationals and Diamondbacks standing between them and a trip to October. That was the low-water mark for this team.
Since that date, the Padres have gone 41-18. They won five straight in late July, six straight in August and eight straight in September. They've lost thrice since Labor Day. The reason for the resurgence? Check out these numbers.
| Padres offensive ranks before and after July 24 | | |
| | Before | After |
| Runs/game | 4.14 (25th) | 4.95 (3rd) |
| AVG | .230 (28th) | .268 (2nd) |
| OBP | .307 (27th) | .339 (2nd) |
| SLG | .383 (27th) | .425 (2nd) |
| OPS | .689 (26th) | .764 (2nd) |
San Diego's offense went from bottom-five to top-five. Some of that is batted-ball luck and sequencing. A lot of it is Fernando Tatis Jr. turning back into a monster. Jackson Merrill had a similar rebirth. Ty France continued his bounce-back campaign. Xander Bogaerts shifted from unwatchable to capable. Unsung heroes such as Dustin Harris and Luis Rengifo got hot. The starting pitching did just enough. The game's best bullpen never stopped dominating. It's that unit, led by a cadre of flamethrowers in Mason Miller, Adrian Morejon and Bradgley Rodriguez, that makes these Padres a particularly formidable October opponent.
X-factors
Cubs: Alex Bregman — specifically, his face
One week ago, Bregman was the victim of some very painful misfortune. A check-swing foul ball off the bat of Cubs first baseman Michael Busch struck Bregman in the face while he was standing in the on-deck circle. Blood dripped from below his left eye as he scurried down the dugout steps into the clubhouse. A trip to the hospital revealed multiple facial fractures. The incident kept Bregman out of the lineup until Friday, when he went 0-for-4 with a strikeout as Chicago's DH. He went 4-for-4 with two home runs and a walk in Sunday's season finale.
There's no doubt that Bregman, the textbook definition of a "grinder," will take the field in October. But at what level? He has been so integral to Chicago's lineup for the past few months that even a slightly reduced version of Bregman could unsettle things. Among active players, only his former Astros teammate Jose Altuve has taken more postseason plate appearances.
Padres: Fernando Tatis Jr.
Nothing is more meaningfully different about this year's Padres team compared to the one that went three and see-ya at Wrigley in 2025 than Fernando Tatis Jr.'s stunning offensive reemergence. Things didn't start so swimmingly this year for the swaggering outfielder, who needed 55 games to clock his first longball of this season. But since May 30, Tatis' .914 OPS ranks fourth in the NL, and his 4.9 fWAR ranks second in MLB behind only Crow-Armstrong.
This version of Tatis looks a lot like the one who took the baseball world by storm en route to finishing third in NL MVP in 2021. Will that brilliance show up in a small October sample? It usually has throughout the 27-year-old's career; he holds a 1.114 postseason OPS in 70 plate appearances. Tatis, though, has never advanced past the NLDS. Remember, he was in PED timeout when the Padres stampeded to the NLCS in 2022. Could this month be his path back to full-blown superstardom?
How they win
Cubs: The margins were razor thin when these teams lined up in the wild-card round last year, with a highlight reel of web gems from shortstop Dansby Swanson making the difference. Those games, oddly enough, were incredibly low-scoring, with Chicago snagging two 3-1 wins and San Diego edging out a 3-0 win. It's hard to imagine the Cubs and their underwhelming relief group winning that way again, particularly on the road. To advance, they'll need buckets of runs. With PCA, Bregman, Seiya Suzuki and Co., that's a real possibility.
Padres: The Padres' formula for success has been the same for the past few seasons: Shorten the game. San Diego realistically needs five innings from its starters. Then manager Craig Stammen gets to turn things over to the best relief core in baseball, led by southpaw Adrían Morejon and flamethrower Mason Miller. The Friars' starting pitching has gotten stronger as they've gotten healthy, so if Michael King in Game 1 and likely Nick Pivetta in Game 2 can each give San Diego 15 outs, the Padres have a good chance of making quick work of Chicago.

item.content:encoded:
As the 2026 MLB postseason prepares to begin, it's a good time for some bold predictions about who will win and why, from the wild-card rounds to the World Series.
Chicago White Sox at Houston Astros
Houston was just 11-13 in September and it felt like neither the Astros nor the Texas Rangers wanted to win the AL West. Houston finally did on the last day, but the Astros aren't inspiring confidence that they can go deep into the postseason.
The White Sox could have been the AL Central champs, but couldn't hang on as Cleveland made a hard charge and overtook them. For a team that has been told all season about they are still living in the shadow of a 121-loss season two years ago, this team has a chip on its shoulder. That should push the White Sox into the next round.
Boston Red Sox at New York Yankees
After a chaotic weather weekend in the Northeast that forced the Red Sox to play Game 162 in Tampa and canceled the final game of the season for the Yankees, that extra day of rest (and far less travel) may help New York when the wild-card series opens in the Bronx.
New York's pitching lineup of Cam Schlittler, Max Fried and Gerrit Cole will be enough to overcome any of the Yankees' offensive issues in a series that will last just two games.
Philadelphia Phillies at Atlanta Braves
Like Houston, Philadelphia did little to inspire confidence in its postseason future at the end of the regular season. It's also been a season where the Braves have Philadelphia's number, winning nine of the 13 games the two rivals have played. Atlanta sweeps Philadelphia.
Chicago Cubs at San Diego Padres
The Padres are red-hot entering the wild card, going 18-6 in September to secure a home series. Having the home fans on their side, San Diego will continue its solid play by sweeping the Cubs into the offseason.
New York Yankees vs. Tampa Bay Rays
While the Yankees may have had enough to get into the ALDS, there's little doubt that the Rays are the better team.
All season, it was a question of if New York could catch Tampa Bay for the AL East title. The Rays kept showing they weren't going to crack under any pressure, and that continues with a 3-1 series win to move on to the ALCS.
Chicago White Sox vs. Cleveland Guardians
Chicago's story has been incredible, but there's a reason why the Guardians won the division ... and keep a reputation as the team that doesn't die easily. They're built for pressure and the postseason and will dispatch the White Sox in four games.
Atlanta Braves vs. Los Angeles Dodgers
This will be must-see TV as two of the NL's behemoths battle it out. The home advantage will make a difference for the Dodgers, who will win in Game 5 to seal another trip to the NLCS.
San Diego Padres vs. Milwaukee Brewers
Milwaukee is for real. There have been plenty of instances in the past where the Brewers have stumbled in the postseason, but this won't be a repeat of those mistakes. Jacob Misiorowski will set the tone in the first game and the Brewers will win in four.
Tampa Bay Rays vs. Cleveland Guardians
The Rays went 5-1 against Cleveland this season. With homefield advantage, there's no reason to think that trend won't continue. Look for the Rays to oust the Guardians in six games.
Los Angeles Dodgers vs. Milwaukee Brewers
This season, the Brewers are 4-3 against the Dodgers. With Milwaukee holding home-field advantage, this is the year that Los Angeles is finally stopped short of winning it all.
There is a lot to like for Milwaukee in their relief pitching options, and it may come down to that. While the Dodgers may have the better rotation, Milwaukee has the better pitching staff overall. Pitching wins in October, and the Brewers win a classic in seven games in front of their home fans.
Tampa Bay Rays vs. Milwaukee Brewers
A World Series without a "major market" in it? Oh this will set up plenty of conversations for what will be a contentious offseason.
Neither of these teams have won a World Series, making for another fascinating storyline in what will be an epic Fall Classic. Milwaukee has the home-field advantage thanks to their 103 regular-season wins, and that makes a big difference in this battle of the top seeds.
Brewers in six.
